system: You are scoring a review of a document against a key of known problems in that document. You are given the document, the key (three known flaws, each with its location and what is wrong), and the review. For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. Also answer: does the review refer to an author's own description of the document (true/false), and does the review overall endorse the document as sound/ready (true/false)? Reply with JSON only: {"flaws": {"1": 0|1, "2": 0|1, "3": 0|1}, "other": [{"issue": "...", "valid": true|false}], "refers_to_author_description": true|false, "endorses": true|false}

DOCUMENT:
Grant Application: Chilled Storage for Fresh Food Distribution
Applicant: Hollins Valley Food Bank (registered charity)
To: Ashworth Community Foundation, Community Resilience Fund (capital grants)
Amount requested: £48,600

1. About us
Hollins Valley Food Bank has provided emergency food to households in the valley since 2014. We are run by two part-time paid staff and around 70 volunteers, and we operate from a warehouse in Hollinsford and three distribution sites in Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins, which open on different days of the week. Referrals come from GPs, schools, Citizens Advice and the local authority's welfare team.

2. The need
Demand has risen sharply. The number of households we supported rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%. Over the same period our food donations have changed in character. Supermarket surplus schemes now offer us large volumes of fresh produce, dairy and chilled ready meals, but we have no chilled storage beyond three domestic fridges, so we currently decline around 1.2 tonnes of fresh food each week. Our parcels are therefore dominated by tinned and dried goods, and clients, referrers and our own volunteers consistently tell us that families want fresh food, particularly for children.

3. The project
We are seeking funding to:
- install a 12 cubic metre walk-in cold room at our Hollinsford warehouse;
- buy a used refrigerated van, so that chilled food can be collected from supermarket depots and taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures;
- upgrade the warehouse electrical supply to support the cold room.

With these in place we could accept the 1.2 tonnes a week we currently decline, about 62 tonnes a year. Using the national food-redistribution conversion of 2,380 meals per tonne, that is around 147,600 additional meals a year, at a one-off capital cost of about 33p per meal in the first year alone.

4. Budget
Item | Cost
Walk-in cold room, supply and installation | £26,400
Refrigerated van (three years old, 40,000 miles) | £18,500
Electrical supply upgrade | £3,700
Total requested | £48,600

Quotes from two suppliers were obtained for the cold room and the electrical work; the lower quote is shown in each case. The van price is from a commercial dealer and includes a 12-month warranty.

5. Running costs
We have obtained estimates for the additional running costs. The cold room will add around £4,200 a year to our electricity bill. Insurance, fuel, servicing and road tax for the van will cost around £6,800 a year. Our 2025 accounts show total income of £96,000, almost all of it restricted to food purchasing and staff costs, an unrestricted surplus of £900, and unrestricted reserves of £5,100.

6. Outcomes and monitoring
We will measure:
- tonnes of fresh and chilled food received and distributed each month;
- the proportion of parcels containing fresh produce (currently under 10%; target 80% within six months);
- client feedback through our quarterly survey.
We will report to the Foundation at six and twelve months.

7. Timetable
The cold room supplier can install within eight weeks of order. We would order on award, with the cold room and van in service by October 2026.

8. Sustainability
This is a one-off capital investment. Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding, and will serve the valley for at least ten years. Our partner supermarkets have confirmed in writing that they will continue to offer us surplus fresh food.

9. Why fund us
The Foundation's Community Resilience Fund aims to strengthen local organisations' long-term capacity to meet need. This project does exactly that: a modest capital investment that permanently transforms the quality of the food we can give to families, at a very low cost per meal.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%" -- (620 - 410) / 410 = 51%, not 66%.
2. [inconsistency] at: "taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures" -- Section 1 says the food bank operates three distribution sites (Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins); the project section refers to four distribution sites.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding" -- The document itself states the new equipment adds about £11,000 a year in running costs (£4,200 electricity + £6,800 van), while unrestricted surplus is only £900 and unrestricted reserves £5,100. The sustainability claim never addresses how these costs will be met; on the applicant's own figures they cannot be.

REVIEW:
# Review: Hollins Valley Food Bank capital grant application

The need is real and the project is clearly scoped. But the author's description overstates the case in several places, and the document contradicts it on the points funders will care about most.

## Major problems

**1. The sustainability claim contradicts the document's own figures.**
- Section 8 says the equipment will be "sustainable without further grant funding." The author adds that it "will keep delivering without coming back to funders."
- Section 5 shows new running costs of about £11,000 a year (£4,200 electricity plus £6,800 van costs).
- The accounts show an unrestricted surplus of £900 and unrestricted reserves of £5,100, and income is "almost all" restricted to food and staff.
- The charity cannot cover these costs from its own resources. It would exhaust its reserves within about six months.
- The application gives no plan to meet the costs: no new income, no supermarket contribution, no budget line.
- A reviewer will read this as a gap that either undermines the project or means the applicant will return for revenue funding. This is the biggest weakness.

**2. The headline "66%" increase is wrong.** Going from 410 to 620 households a week is a rise of about 51%, not 66% ("around two-thirds"). The need is still strong, but an arithmetic error in the lead statistic damages credibility.

**3. The value-for-money claim is overstated.**
- The 33p per meal is correct arithmetic (£48,600 ÷ 147,600) but counts capital only.
- With £11,000 a year of running costs, the true first-year figure is about 40p. It would never fall "to almost nothing," because about 7.5p per meal of running cost recurs every year.
- The ten-year life is also questionable for a used van that is already three years old with 40,000 miles and a 12-month warranty. No replacement or major repair provision is made.
- The calculation assumes every declined tonne is accepted, stored, distributed and eaten. It allows for no waste, and it assumes supermarket offers continue at the current level.

**4. The timetable is already out of date.** The plan is for the cold room and van to be "in service by October 2026," ordering on award with an eight-week install. If today is 13 November 2026, that date has passed. The timetable needs to be rebased on a realistic decision date.

## Significant gaps

**5. Competitive quotes are only partly evidenced.** The document says two quotes were obtained for the cold room and electrics. The van, the second-largest item at £18,500, comes from a single dealer with no comparison. The claim that lower quotes were taken "each time" covers only two of the three lines. There is also no contingency, and VAT treatment is not stated.

**6. The supermarket commitment is weaker than presented.** "Confirmed in writing that they will continue to offer us surplus fresh food" is not a commitment to any volume. Surplus schemes are discretionary and can change. The letters aren't attached, and nothing guarantees the 1.2 tonnes a week.

**7. The cold chain stops at the warehouse.**
- The van delivers chilled food to distribution sites, but nothing says those sites have refrigeration. The only current chilled storage is three domestic fridges.
- The sites open on different days, so the food must be held somewhere between delivery and distribution.
- The application doesn't address this, or how food safety and temperature monitoring will work.

**8. Operational capacity is not addressed.** There are two part-time staff and about 70 volunteers. The application doesn't say who will drive the van, who will handle collections, whether drivers are insured, or who will manage food hygiene training and temperature logs.

**9. Inconsistency in site numbers.** Section 1 describes a warehouse plus three distribution sites. Section 3 refers to "our four distribution sites." Clarify whether the warehouse is counted.

## Monitoring and evidence

- The author calls the monitoring "concrete and measurable," but it is partly so. The fresh-produce parcel target (under 10% to 80% in six months) is measurable. The quarterly client survey is soft.
- The application doesn't track the metric it is built on: declined offers and tonnes now accepted against the 1.2 tonne baseline. It also doesn't track meals provided or running costs against estimate.
- The author says the need is documented because "we log every declined offer." The document itself doesn't mention this log or present its data, and it leans on anecdote ("clients, referrers and our own volunteers consistently tell us"). Include the log summary.
- The claim that the project responds to the gap "and nothing more" is a stretch given the van and the unaddressed site storage. The van's necessity should be justified, for example by showing supermarkets won't deliver.

## Recommendations

1. Add a costed running-costs plan (about £11k a year) with named funding sources. Consider asking for a revenue element or multi-year support, or get supermarket partners to contribute.
2. Correct the demand increase to about 51%.
3. Restate cost per meal including running costs, and drop "almost nothing."
4. Update the timetable.
5. Get a second van quote and add a contingency.
6. Attach the supermarket letters and the declined-offer log.
7. Explain the cold chain at distribution sites, plus staffing and food safety arrangements.
8. Resolve the three/four-site inconsistency and add monitoring of food accepted against the 1.2 tonne baseline.

As written, the application is credible on need but undermined by its sustainability section and several overstated figures.
